text: Chapter 16 says the value of a representation invariant is not that it is true, but something else. What?
choices: That it can be verified automatically by the compiler at each mutation point.
That it makes the class immutable, since an invariant forbids state changes.
That the code able to break it is small enough to check — the invariant scopes your reasoning to one class.
That it documents the data structure for readers who have not seen the implementation.
explanation: An invariant nobody could violate needs no protection; an invariant anyone could violate is not a guarantee. The value is the boundary: if the fields are private, the only code that can break the promise is the code in this file, and that is a finite thing you can read. Chapter 19 supplies `private` as the mechanism and Liskov's argument for why a convention anyone can reach around does not count.
